prompt.context: Our client is a global luxury cruise line. It buys ships and offers tours around the world to individuals on vacations. The board noticed that the ROIC (Return On Invested Capital) is not at the same level as competitors. The client is the #2 player and has $8 billion in revenues and is half as big as the #1 player.
prompt.question: Our client wants to know what strategy to use to obtain double-digit ROIC in the next 2 to 3 years. How would you analyze this problem?

clarifying_info.q: What are the current financials — revenues, operating costs, and invested capital?
What price does the client charge per customer per day versus competitors?
clarifying_info.a: The client earns an average of $250 per day per customer (including ticket and on-board spend); competitors average $260 per day per customer.

clarifying_info.q: Does the competitor target a higher income segment than our customers?
clarifying_info.a: No — both target the same income segment.

clarifying_info.q: Are we comparable to competitors in terms of brand and quality?
clarifying_info.a: Yes — in fact the client is considered more premium than its main competitor.

clarifying_info.q: Does the client currently operate at full capacity?
clarifying_info.a: Not initially at regular prices. The company discounts heavily in the days or weeks before each departure in order to fill ships to full capacity.

framework: Define ROIC: (Revenue - Operating Costs) / Invested Capital
Calculate current ROIC and gap to double-digit target
Revenue drivers: pricing, volume/capacity utilization, new routes/markets
Cost drivers: fixed costs (ships, depreciation, crew) vs. variable costs (fuel, food, port fees); benchmark vs. competitors
Pricing strategy: ticket price vs. on-board spend, discount policy, demand elasticity
Capacity strategy: full-capacity obsession vs. profit-maximizing occupancy rate

questions.guidance: Apply ROIC = (Revenue - Operating Costs) / Invested Capital. Current ROIC is 5%, well below a double-digit target.

questions.prompt: If the only lever is reducing operating costs, how much must costs fall to reach 10% ROIC?
questions.guidance: Set ROIC = 10% and solve for the new operating cost level. The required cost reduction is approximately 10%.

questions.prompt: If the only lever is growing revenues, how much must revenues increase to reach 10% ROIC?
questions.guidance: Set ROIC = 10% and solve for the new revenue level. Revenue must grow ~9%.

questions.prompt: The client earns $250/day per customer vs. the competitor's $260/day. The client is considered more premium. What does this imply, and what deeper pricing issue should you explore?
questions.guidance: A strong candidate notes the paradox: a more-premium brand earns less per customer. This suggests either underpricing on the ticket or lower on-board spend. The deeper issue is the heavy last-minute discounting practice. Because the industry is obsessed with sailing at full capacity, it discounts aggressively before departure — which trains customers to wait for lower prices, reducing average realized revenue per customer and compressing margins. The profit-maximizing approach would be to hold prices firm and accept 70-80% capacity rather than discount to 100%, because variable costs (food, port fees, etc.) also fall with lower occupancy.

math.setup: Revenue gap per customer per day = $260 - $250 = $10
steps: Closing the gap partially (not fully discounting) would lift average realized revenue
math.answer: $10/day/customer gap; eliminating last-minute discounting is the primary pricing lever

brainstorming.prompt: What specific levers — on both the revenue and cost side — could the client use to reach double-digit ROIC in 2-3 years?

categories.name: Revenue — Pricing
ideas: Eliminate or sharply reduce last-minute discounting to stop training customers to wait for deals
Introduce dynamic/yield-management pricing (similar to airlines) to optimize realized revenue
Raise base ticket prices given premium positioning vs. competitor
Introduce premium cabin tiers or upsell packages

categories.name: Revenue — On-board Spend
ideas: Expand on-board offerings (specialty dining, excursions, spa, entertainment)
Bundle on-board credits into ticket price to increase perceived value and spend
Loyalty programs that reward higher on-board spend

categories.name: Revenue — Volume & Routes
ideas: Add new routes or itineraries in high-demand regions
Increase fleet utilization (shorter turnaround times in port)
Target new geographies or customer segments (e.g., emerging-market high-net-worth)

categories.name: Cost — Variable Costs
ideas: Fuel hedging to reduce fuel cost volatility
Renegotiate port and docking fees
Optimize food and beverage procurement through volume contracts
Accept lower-than-100% occupancy to cut variable costs (food, services) that scale with passengers

categories.name: Cost — Fixed Costs
ideas: Fleet rationalization — retire older, less fuel-efficient ships
Benchmark crew-to-passenger ratios against competitors
Consolidate back-office and administrative functions
Explore shared services or outsourcing for non-core functions

categories.name: Best Practices from Competitors
ideas: Study #1 player's pricing and capacity management practices
Adopt revenue management systems used by airlines or hotels
Benchmark marketing spend and channel mix

recommendation: Address both the revenue gap (~9% needed) and cost gap (~10% needed) simultaneously rather than relying on one lever alone

The single highest-impact initiative is to reform the pricing and capacity strategy: stop last-minute deep discounting, implement yield-management pricing, and accept operating at 70-80% capacity rather than discounting to full capacity — this alone can narrow the $10/day/customer revenue gap vs. competitors while also lowering variable costs at lower occupancy
Complement pricing reform with targeted cost reduction (fuel efficiency, procurement, fleet rationalization) to close the remaining gap
risks: Industry norm of full-capacity obsession may create competitive pressure to revert to discounting if competitors do not follow suit
Demand may be more elastic than expected even among premium travelers, so price increases could reduce volume beyond the break-even point
Cost reduction programs (crew rationalization, ship retirements) risk damaging service quality and the premium brand
2-3 year timeline is tight if structural changes (new pricing systems, fleet changes) require long lead times
next_steps: Conduct detailed revenue management analysis: model profit at 70%, 80%, 90% occupancy vs. 100% with discounting to quantify the optimal capacity/price trade-off
Benchmark variable cost structure against the #1 player to identify specific cost-reduction opportunities
Pilot the no-discount pricing policy on 2-3 routes and measure impact on realized revenue and profitability
Develop a multi-year fleet efficiency roadmap (fuel, maintenance, potential ship retirement)
Assess pricing system and IT capabilities required to implement dynamic yield management
